chunk_findings.detail: `row["recall"] = kind.recall and kind.stored_kind` returns the value of `stored_kind` when both operands are truthy, not a boolean. Since `stored_kind` is the stored kind string, a declared kind with `recall=True` and `stored_kind="task"` produces `row["recall"] == "task"`. `audit()` then hits `if isinstance(have, str): continue`, treating the value as a descriptor-declined reason, so it never reports a missing recall capability or a stale recall exemption; `render()` prints `declined` instead of `yes`. The probe should coerce to `bool(...)` (and probably verify the stored kind against `_recall_tables()`).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/records/parity.py::declared_row

chunk_findings.detail: The audit matrix omits the agent permission route even though the stated rule `r-record-parity` extends `D-correction-permissions-2` and the intent requires the matrix to cover the agent permission route. The `Reading` section explicitly says the permission route is “Not measured,” so the table and the parity test have no capability column or exemption mechanism for it. Concrete failure: add a kind that has `mcp=yes`, `context=yes`, and `export=yes` but no agent permission route; because `tests/test_record_parity.py` only enumerates the 18 listed columns, the test still passes and no gap task is filed, despite the kind violating `r-record-parity`.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/research/record-parity.md:Reading

chunk_findings.detail: `test_a_stale_exemption_is_reported` does not actually create a stale exemption; it only forces `append` to `True` for rows that are in `R.KINDS`. If `P.EXEMPT` contains no append exemption (for example after append support is implemented for every kind and the append exemptions are removed), then `P.audit({**rows, **fixed})` has no append gap and no append exemption to report, so it returns no append problem and the assertion fails. This makes the test fail on a valid, improved parity state instead of testing stale-exemption detection.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_record_parity.py:49

chunk_findings.detail: `test_an_unlisted_gap_is_reported` assumes `risk:edit` is not exempted. If the current matrix has `rows["risk"]["edit"]` false but exempted in `P.EXEMPT` (a state allowed by the parity rule and one that would make `test_no_unexempted_gap_and_no_stale_exemption` pass), then `broken` is not an unlisted gap; `P.audit(broken)` will not contain `"risk: lacks edit"` and the test fails. The test should remove the exemption with `monkeypatch` or choose a capability/kind pair that is not exempted.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_record_parity.py:44

chunk_findings.detail: The matrix omits the required agent permission route capability. The stated intent requires the parity matrix to cover “agent permission route” for every kind, and this note cites `D-correction-permissions-2`, but the table has no such column and the Reading explicitly says it is “Not measured”. Concretely, a kind such as `pack` can have no agent permission route and still pass the parity audit because there is no capability column or test for that route. This is wrong because the audit is supposed to detect every required capability gap, including permission-route gaps, rather than relying on an unmeasured claim that “correct tasks” cover it. [D-correction-permissions-2]
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/research/record-parity.md:Reading

chunk_findings.detail: The `pending` state makes the `correct` capability permanently unenforceable. The legend defines `pending` as “never failed either way”, and every row in the table uses `pending` for `correct`. If `REC-correct-surface` is abandoned, delayed, or otherwise never lands, `ddflow correct` remains absent today, yet the parity test still cannot fail for any kind because `pending` is neither a gap nor a stale-exemption failure. This contradicts the stated requirement that the test fail when a kind lacks a capability without a listed exemption with a reason.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/research/record-parity.md:Legend

chunk_findings.detail: The test only passes when there is already at least one `append` exemption for a row whose name is in `R.KINDS`. It creates `fixed` by setting `append: True` for those rows and then asserts that `P.audit({**rows, **fixed})` contains a message with `"append"`. If append parity has been achieved for all RecordKinds, so `P.EXEMPT` contains no kind-row `append` exemption, then `fixed` does not create a stale exemption, `P.audit(rows)` is `[]` by the preceding test, and `P.audit({**rows, **fixed})` is also `[]`; the assertion fails. Thus closing the append gaps makes this “stale exemption” test fail, and stale append exemptions for non-RecordKind rows are not exercised at all.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_record_parity.py:test_a_stale_exemption_is_reported (lines 47-49)

chunk_findings.detail: The test hard-codes `risk`/`edit` and assumes that pair is not exempted. If a valid exemption exists for that gap, for example `P.EXEMPT["risk:edit"] = "task-123: close risk edit"` while `rows["risk"]["edit"] is False`, then `broken` still has an exempted gap. The audit must not report `"risk: lacks edit"` in that state (otherwise `test_no_unexempted_gap_and_no_stale_exemption` would fail), so the `any(...)` assertion fails even though the audit is behaving as specified. The test needs to remove or avoid exemptions for the injected gap rather than relying on `risk:edit` being unexempted.

chunk_findings.detail: `audit`’s per-kind stale check treats a global `@engine:<cap>` exemption as stale for any single declared kind that has the capability. `_exact` returns true whenever `("@engine", cap)` is in `EXEMPT`, and `_exemption` returns that reason for every declared kind. Given two declared kinds, if one row has `append` (or `merge`, `split`, `supersede`, `restore`, `export`, `change_feed`, `context`) true while another row has it false and relies on the same `@engine` exemption, the audit emits a message like `name: has append, delete its exemption (RP-gap-append-verb)`. That is wrong because deleting the exemption would make the second kind an unexempted gap; only `_stale`’s global check should decide when an `@engine` exemption is stale, and it correctly requires every declared kind to have or decline the capability.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/records/parity.py::audit [r-record-parity]

chunk_findings.detail: Blanket kind exemptions are never reported stale. The module doc says the exemption list is a ratchet and that an exemption for a kind that no longer lacks a capability is itself a failure. For the existing `("rule", "*")` exemption, `_exemption` returns the blanket reason, but `_exact` is false because only `(rule, "*")` is in `EXEMPT`, not `(rule, cap)`; `_stale` has no case for a declared kind’s `*` exemption. If `rows["rule"]` has every non-pending capability true, `audit` still reports no stale `rule` exemption, so the exemption can persist after the kind no longer lacks any measured capability.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/records/parity.py::_exact [r-record-parity]

chunk_findings.detail: The Reading says that for kinds not yet in the engine, “declare the kind and the capabilities follow from the engine.” But the same document states that the generic `record` surface offers only `list show add edit remove search revise history`, and that `merge`, `split`, `supersede`, and `restore` are not offered, while `append` is also missing. The matrix itself shows some non-`RecordKind` kinds already have those capabilities: `bug` has `merge` and `restore` yes, and `task` has `append`, `merge`, and `split` yes. If `RP-engine-bug` or `RP-engine-task` is done as the doc describes before the engine-wide lifecycle/append gaps are closed, those kinds would lose capabilities they currently have; if the engine-wide gaps are prerequisites, the doc omits that dependency and misstates the per-kind gap. This is a concrete task-ordering failure: landing the per-kind engine task first regresses parity instead of improving it.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/research/record-parity.md:49

chunk_findings.detail: The test named `test_declaring_a_legacy_kind_requires_deleting_its_row` does not actually declare a legacy row as a kind. `monkeypatch.setitem(R.KINDS, "task", R.KINDS["risk"])` replaces the value already stored under the existing key `"task"`; it does not add a new key to `R.KINDS`. If the audit reports a legacy row that has become a kind because that row's name now appears in `R.KINDS` (which is what “declaring a kind” means and what the message “delete its LEGACY row” implies), the monkeypatch cannot create the condition: the set of keys in `R.KINDS` is unchanged, and `task` was already present before the test. Conversely, if the audit somehow inspects the kind object's internal legacy flag, the test would depend on `R.KINDS["risk"]` itself being legacy, which would make the clean matrix fail in `test_no_unexempted_gap_and_no_stale_exemption`. Thus this test either cannot trigger the reported problem or is testing a different, unspecified condition, giving false confidence that legacy-row declaration is audited.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_record_parity.py:61-63

chunk_findings.detail: `row["recall"] = kind.recall and kind.stored_kind` returns the stored-kind string itself when the kind has recall, not a boolean. For a declared kind with `kind.recall` truthy and `kind.stored_kind == "tasks"`, `declared_row(name)["recall"]` is `"tasks"`. `audit` treats any string as a descriptor-declared declined reason (`if isinstance(have, str): continue`), and `render` prints `"declined"` for any string, so a kind that actually has recall is misreported as declined and can also bypass stale-exemption checks for an exact recall exemption.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/records/parity.py:declared_row

chunk_findings.detail: The per-kind stale check in `audit` treats `@engine` exact exemptions as if they were kind-specific exemptions. Because `_exact(name, cap)` is true for every declared kind whenever `("@engine", cap)` exists, `audit` reports `name: has cap, delete its exemption` as soon as one declared kind has the capability, even though the global `@engine` exemption is still required for other declared kinds. For example, with `EXEMPT[("@engine", "merge")]` present and rows `{"a": {"merge": True, ...}, "b": {"merge": False, ...}}`, `audit` fails with a stale exemption for `a`, although deleting `@engine merge` would make `b` fail.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/records/parity.py:audit

chunk_findings.detail: `audit` does not detect stale kind-specific exemptions when the kind is no longer present in the matrix. `audit` loops only over `rows`, and `_stale` checks only `@engine`, `@legacy:*`, and `@defs` scopes. If `KINDS` no longer contains `proposal`, but `EXEMPT[("proposal", "history")]` remains, `audit()` returns no problem for that exemption, so the ratchet can silently retain an exemption for a kind that no longer exists.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/records/parity.py:audit

chunk_findings.detail: The legend makes `correct` and `agent_permission` non-failing states ("reported, never failed in either state"), although line 3 says the test fails on any unexempted gap or stale exemption and the capabilities list includes both. For example, `gate` (line 32) has `agent_permission=pending` while it is not a RecordKind and has no agent-permission route; if `ddflow correct` is abandoned or the route is never implemented, the matrix remains pending and the test passes, so the audit cannot enforce parity or detect the stale pending exemption.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/research/record-parity.md:5

chunk_findings.detail: The test monkeypatches `P.EXEMPT` to a single stale-exemption key `("@engine", "append")`, but then only forces `append` to `True` for rows whose names are in `R.KINDS`. If `@engine` is a legacy/non-`RecordKind` row (which is the natural reading of the `@` key and the audit’s legacy handling) and its `append` cell is false, `fixed` leaves that row unchanged. `P.audit` then sees an exemption for a row that still lacks `append`, so it is not stale, and the assertion fails. The stale-exemption test should force the specific exempted row’s capability to true regardless of whether that row is currently in `R.KINDS`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_record_parity.py: test_a_stale_exemption_is_reported

chunk_findings.detail: The test checks `recall` and `search` only for names in `R.KINDS`, but the stated audit requirement includes kinds that are not yet `RecordKinds` (`gate`, `template`, `lens`, `role`, `pack`, `job`). If `P.matrix()` returns a non-boolean cell for one of those non-`RecordKind` rows, such as `rows["gate"]["recall"] = "not yet"` or `rows["gate"]["search"] = None`, this test passes because `gate` is absent from `R.KINDS`, while the parity matrix still contains an invalid/non-boolean capability cell. The test should iterate over `rows`, not only `R.KINDS`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_record_parity.py: test_recall_and_search_cells_are_booleans

chunk_findings.detail: `matrix()` first builds rows for every declared kind, then unconditionally overwrites any same-named row with `legacy_row()`. Thus, in the state the audit is explicitly designed to detect — a `LEGACY` row whose name is also in `KINDS` — the audit evaluates the declared kind using the legacy probes instead of its descriptor. For example, monkeypatch `KINDS` to include `"task"` while `LEGACY` still contains the task row. If the declared task descriptor provides `history` but the legacy task row does not, `matrix()["task"]["history"]` is `False`; `scopes()` then returns `("@engine", "task")`, so the `@legacy:task` exemption is not considered, and `audit()` reports `task: lacks history and no exemption names the task` even though the declared kind has it. The reverse can hide a real gap: if the descriptor lacks `merge` but the legacy `task fold` probe exists, the matrix row says `True`, and `audit()` may even report the `@engine merge` exemption stale while the declared kind still lacks `merge`. The stale legacy row should be reported without replacing the declared row.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/records/parity.py::matrix
